## 1. Answers to the 11 questions

**Q1 — default-bridge DNS gap:** 
```
--- resolv.conf ---
# Generated by Docker Engine.
# This file can be edited; Docker Engine will not make further changes once it
# has been modified.

nameserver 192.168.65.7

# Based on host file: '/etc/resolv.conf' (legacy)
# Overrides: []
--- dig db ---
--- getent ---
not found
```
`dig db` comes back empty because there is no record of ‘db’ in the DNS record table of the DNS server (192.168.65.7) provided by the Docker default bridge network. Docker’s embedded DNS server on a default bridge network will not create records for container names so communication between its containers will not be able to resolve container names, so it only serves regular requests like internet requests.
However, on a a user-defined bridge, docker will record container names thus allowing its containers to resolve and communicate using their container names as hostname.


**Q2 — db IP after restart + why hard-coding is wrong:** 

`DB_IP was 172.17.0.2, now 172.17.0.2`
The IP did not change after restart. 
Hard-coding an IP address and absence of DNS are technically the same bug because both situations means that the application will depend on a specific IP address. If the container is recreated, it will have a new IP and the application will not find the newly created container because it is trying to communicate using the old IP and no dynamic way of resolving containers.
Using this approach reliably would mean having to manually manage IP addresses of container and updating the configurations of applications accordingly whenever the IP changes. This approach is not efficient as it will be difficult to manually maintain and update IP addresses and scalability will be difficult as containers are created and deleted.

**Q3 — subnet/gateway + flags to control them:** 
```
[
  {
    "Subnet": "172.20.0.0/16",
    "Gateway": "172.20.0.1"
  }
]
```
The subnet and gateway can be controlled using the `—subnet` flag to control the subnet, and `—gateway` to control/specify the gateway.

**Q4 — user-defined bridge DNS + design implication:** 
```
--- dig db ---
172.20.0.2
--- dig api ---
172.20.0.3
--- curl api ---
ok
```

`dig db` now returns the IP address of the db container as opposed to no result in part 1. Since the containers are on a user-defined bridge network, the Docker’s DNS server records and resolve containers hostname with the container name. 
In a 10-service stack, each service will only need the names of the rest of the other services to communicate since Docker user-defined bridge network will automatically resolve those names to the respective IP addresses. if in a default bridge network, each service would need to know the IP addresses of every other service, and this will need to be updated with every IP change of any other service making the system fragile and difficult to maintain. 

**Q5 — what isolated the stranger + how to bridge it:** 

cohort-net, which is a user-defined bridge network provided the isolation because it is a separate layer network with its own DNS namespace. 
To reach db from cohort-other, both containers must share at least a network. Either connect db into cohort-other network (`docker network connect cohort-other db`) or connect the stranger container into cohort-net with `docker network connect cohort-net <stranger-container>`

**Q6 — `-p HOST:CONTAINER` semantics:**

The 3rd probe failed because it is making a request to the api container on port 18080 of the api container which is where api is not listening to requests on. The mapping `-p 18080:8080` is only for host-container port mapping, meaning the 18080 port is only meant for requests coming from outside docker to reach the api container. So another container trying to reach api will not get anything on port 18080 but must use 8080 to successfully reach api.
-p HOST:CONTAINER actually forwards request from the host’s port into the container port, not changing the container’s listening port. `pfctl -s nat 2>/dev/null` shows the NAT rule that represents the host-to-container forwarding. 

**Q7 — `docker rm -v` vs named-volume behavior:** 

No, `docker container rm -fv` did not delete cohort-db-data because the `-v` flag on docker container rm removes only the anonymous random volume that is created with the container and does not remove named volumes that were purposely created and attached. An anonymous  volume is created when a container is created and is bound to the lifecycle of that container, but a named volume remains when a container is removed and can only be explicitly deleted using `docker volume rm`.

**Q8 — bind vs named volume + why not to poke the mountpoint:**

With a bind mount, you can mount a specific host directory unto a container hence you can edit and manage files in the container using tools in the host. Also, bind mount allows sharing of configuration files between host and container. However, Docker manages a named volume so thus it can be migrated from one host to another without having to worry about permission issues. Named volume is preferred in production for application data because it is managed by docker thus providing persistence where the stored data is not affected by a change in the host file system.
The host path of a named volume Mountpoint is implemented and managed by Docker internally and will need root permission to access it. Accessing or modifying this mountpoint may result in consistency and permission issues and may also corrupt application data. 

**Q9 — when tmpfs is the right choice:** 

Tmpfs is the right choice for workloads where temporary storage is needed like application data cache. 
Tmpfs consumes less resources over time because it stores data in memory unlike named volume or bind mount that stores in disk. Also with tmpfs there is a guarantee that sensitive data will not be exposed after container is removed.

**Q10 — stopping db before backup + production alternative:**

Stopping db before backing up prevents corrupted backup that may occur in the writing process when the file is being copied. When data is being modified during backup, the files that have been copied files may not be consistent with the actual database state when they are restored. In a production environment, tools such as pg_basebackup (often together with Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) archiving or streaming replication) supports online and consistent backup processes without risking filesystem consistency.

**Q11 — compose-managed network/volume + external:true:**

Docker compose creates a network with name `assignment-04_cohort-net`. This network is different from the one I created by hand in Part 2 as it is the network is based on the context the compose file is in (assignment-04).
Adding `external: true` tells docker to use an existing volume instead of creating one. This can prevent a real outage because `docker compose down -v` removes docker compose-managed volumes, but does not remove external volumes thus, the production database can survive the application stack being torn down and recreated without losing its data.

## 3. Files

### `api/Dockerfile`
```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1.7
FROM python:3.11.15-slim AS build
RUN python -m venv /opt/venv
ENV PATH=/opt/venv/bin:$PATH
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

FROM python:3.11.15-slim AS runtime
RUN useradd --uid 1000 --create-home app
COPY --from=build /opt/venv /opt/venv
ENV PATH=/opt/venv/bin:$PATH
WORKDIR /app
COPY app.py .
EXPOSE 8080
USER app
CMD ["gunicorn", "-b", "0.0.0.0:8080", "app:app"]
```

### `api/app.py`
```python
import os, time
import psycopg2
from flask import Flask, request, jsonify

app = Flask(__name__)

DB_HOST = os.environ.get("DB_HOST", "db")
DB_USER = os.environ.get("DB_USER", "cohort")
DB_PASS = os.environ.get("DB_PASS", "cohort")
DB_NAME = os.environ.get("DB_NAME", "cohort")


def connect():
    for _ in range(30):
        try:
            return psycopg2.connect(
                host=DB_HOST, user=DB_USER, password=DB_PASS, dbname=DB_NAME
            )
        except psycopg2.OperationalError:
            time.sleep(1)
    raise RuntimeError("db never came up")


@app.before_request
def ensure_schema():
    if getattr(app, "_ready", False):
        return
    with connect() as c, c.cursor() as cur:
        cur.execute(
            "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS notes (id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, body TEXT NOT NULL)"
        )
        c.commit()
    app._ready = True


@app.get("/notes")
def list_notes():
    with connect() as c, c.cursor() as cur:
        cur.execute("SELECT id, body FROM notes ORDER BY id")
        return jsonify([{"id": i, "body": b} for i, b in cur.fetchall()])


@app.post("/notes")
def add_note():
    body = request.json.get("body", "")
    with connect() as c, c.cursor() as cur:
        cur.execute("INSERT INTO notes (body) VALUES (%s) RETURNING id", (body,))
        c.commit()
        return jsonify({"id": cur.fetchone()[0], "body": body}), 201


@app.get("/healthz")
def healthz():
    return ("ok", 200)
```

### `compose.yml`
```yaml
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: cohort
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: cohort
      POSTGRES_DB: cohort
    volumes:
      - cohort-db-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U cohort"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 5
    networks:
      - cohort-net

  api:
    image: cohort-api:0.1.0
    environment:
      DB_HOST: db
    ports:
      - "18080:8080"
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
    networks:
      - cohort-net

networks:
  cohort-net:

volumes:
  cohort-db-data:
    external: true   # reuse the volume from Part 4
```

## 5. One trade-off I had to make

(2–4 sentences. Pick **one** decision where the slides offered multiple options and you had to choose: named volume vs bind mount for the db, host network mode vs `-p`, compose vs raw docker commands, etc. Explain why you chose what you chose and what you'd give up by picking the other.)

I used the named volume for the db because it is internally managed by docker so there won't be any issues with persisting data accross different containers/container lifecycle. Also, not worrying about permission issues. The tradeoff is that I am not able to make changes to data or files writen into the named volume directly from the host which would have been able to do if it was a bind mount.
